pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1133, inhabited without a break since, where the divine office has been sung for nearly nine centuries)
etymology: German Heiligenkreuz, holy cross, from the relic given by Duke Leopold V.
biblical_def: Heiligenkreuz in the Vienna woods was founded in 1133 by Leopold III of Babenberg and settled from Morimond, and it takes its name from a relic of the cross brought back by Leopold V. It is the oldest continuously inhabited Cistercian house in the world: the community has never been dispersed, not by Joseph II's suppressions, not by the Turks who reached its walls twice, not by the Nazi government that seized the buildings in 1940, and the seven hours of the divine office have been sung in its choir for nearly nine centuries. The chapter house holds the Babenberg tombs. The dictionary records Heiligenkreuz not for its relic, which belongs with the corruptions, but for that unbroken recitation, because continuance in prayer is commanded in terms that admit no interval, “Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17). The apostolic word for the practice is a verb of persistence with thanksgiving attached, “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2). The posture is a watchman's through a long night, “My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6), and the access that makes such persistence reasonable is open to every believer and needs no choir, “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the office in this sense as a formulary of devotion; a choir as the part of a church where the singers are placed; matins as morning worship; vigils as devotional watching; and to intercede as to plead in favor of another.
webster_full: OFFICE, n. A formulary of devotion; the daily service of the breviary; also, duty, employment.
CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; also, the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
MATINS, n. Morning worship or service; morning prayers or songs.
VIGIL, n. Watch; devotional watching; the eve or day preceding a church festival.
BREVIARY, n. A book containing the daily service of the Roman Catholic or Greek church.
scriptures: Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;
My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
corruption_summary: The oldest continuously inhabited Cistercian house in the world, founded 1133, where the office has been sung without a break.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that persistence in prayer is commanded and that nine centuries of it is therefore not excessive. Heiligenkreuz has never missed the hours, and the apostolic instruction is given without a stated limit, “Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17).

The live temptation is the one Heiligenkreuz's name carries: the house was endowed around a fragment of wood, and a relic proposes to supply an access already granted. Scripture gives the practice its proper companion, “and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2), its proper posture, “more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6), and its proper ground, which is a throne approached directly and boldly, “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16).

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1138, keeping a Gothic cloister with lavabo and the Bear Skin foundation book)
etymology: Middle High German zwetl, from a Slavic root for a clearing or a confluence.
biblical_def: Zwettl in the Waldviertel was founded in 1138 by Hadmar of Kuenring and settled from Heiligenkreuz, and it keeps the most complete Cistercian cloister in Austria, with a Romanesque chapter house and a nine-sided lavabo where the monks washed before meals. Its great treasure is a book: the Bärenhaut or Bear Skin, the abbey's thirteenth-century cartulary, bound in hide and containing the foundation charters, the genealogy of the Kuenrings and the earliest coloured drawings of the family. It has been inhabited since 1138. The dictionary records Zwettl for that habit of writing the title deeds down and keeping them, which is the civil equivalent of a doctrine Scripture states as a command: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). The prophetic complaint against a people is that they left marked ways for unmarked ones, “to walk in paths, in a way not cast up” (Jer 18:15), and the exchange is described as trading a spring for a leaking tank, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13). Yet a cartulary is not the thing itself, and God tells a religious people what He actually wants kept, “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cartulary as a register book of a monastery; a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; a lavatory in this sense is a place for washing; a charter as a written instrument of grant; and a genealogy as an account of descent.
webster_full: CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; a place where papers or records are kept.
LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm or estate may be known and preserved.
LAVATORY, n. A place for washing; a wash-bowl or basin.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or contract.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
corruption_summary: Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1138 with Austria's most complete cloister and the thirteenth-century Bear Skin cartulary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that boundaries written down are a mercy to those who come after. Zwettl bound its charters in hide and kept them for eight hundred years, and the command behind such care is given about field boundaries and holds for every kind, “Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28).

The live temptation is to let the register become the religion, which is the characteristic disease of a landed abbey. Jeremiah describes drift as a preference for unmarked roads, “they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths” (Jer 18:15), and names the trade as a spring for a cracked cistern, “broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). What God says He wants kept is not the parchment, “and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6).

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1202, the largest medieval monastic complex in Austria)
etymology: German Lilienfeld, the field of lilies, from Lilie and Feld.
biblical_def: Lilienfeld in Lower Austria was founded in 1202 by Leopold VI of Babenberg and settled from Heiligenkreuz, and it is the largest medieval monastic complex in the country: a church of the transitional Romanesque-Gothic kind, a cloister with a dormitory above it, a chapter house, and the finest surviving Cistercian library hall of its date in Austria. Leopold VI is buried in the chapter house. The community has been there, with one interruption under Joseph II, since 1202. The dictionary records Lilienfeld for its name, which is a figure Scripture also uses and uses against the builders of monuments. A field of lilies is beautiful and brief, and the prophet sets that brevity directly against the one thing that is not brief, “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter applies the figure to human glory of every sort, including the ecclesiastical, “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass” (1Pe 1:24). The psalmist uses it of a man's whole span, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), which leaves a founder exactly one prayer worth praying over his foundation, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lily as a plant of the genus Lilium; a flower as the blossom of a plant; to fade as to lose colour or freshness; to wither as to fade, to dry up; and to establish as to set and fix firmly.
webster_full: LILY, n. A plant and flower of the genus Lilium, of many species; a flower of great beauty.
FLOWER, n. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of generation; the blossom.
FADE, v.i. To lose color; to lose freshness or vigor; to languish; to decay.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
ESTABLISH, v.t. To set and fix firmly or unalterably; to settle permanently.
scriptures: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
corruption_summary: Lower Austria's Cistercian abbey of 1202, the largest medieval monastic complex in the country, named for a field of lilies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the abbey's own name hands over. A field of lilies is lovely and short-lived, and the prophet sets that brevity against the single thing that outlasts it, “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

The live temptation for the largest complex in a country is to read its own scale as permanence. Peter will not allow the reading, and includes every human distinction in the flower, “and the flower thereof falleth away” (1Pe 1:24). The psalmist says the same of a lifetime, “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15), so a founder is left one petition rather than a monument, “the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17).

pos: n. (the Carinthian Cistercian abbey of 1142, home of the chronicler John of Viktring, afterwards a school)
etymology: Latin Victoringa, from a Roman estate name Victorinus; German Viktring.
biblical_def: Viktring near Klagenfurt was founded in 1142 by Count Bernhard of Spanheim and settled from Villers in Brabant, the first Cistercian house in Carinthia. Its best-known member is John of Viktring, abbot from 1312, whose Liber certarum historiarum is a chief source for Austrian and Carinthian affairs under the Habsburgs and the Luxemburgs. The abbey was dissolved by Joseph II in 1786, used as a cloth factory, and is now a school, with the Romanesque church and its sixteenth-century glass kept in use. The dictionary records Viktring for its two successive trades, chronicling and teaching, which are the same trade: handing on what one received. The duty is domestic before it is institutional, and the hours named for it are ordinary ones, “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7). The psalmist makes the refusal to withhold a positive act, “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4). What is handed on begins with a disposition rather than a syllabus, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10), and the understanding it yields is measured in obedience, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicler as a writer of a chronicle; a school as a place of instruction; to teach as to instruct, to inform; a tutor as one who has the care of instruction; and wisdom as the right use of knowledge.
webster_full: CHRONICLER, n. A writer of a chronicle; a recorder of events in the order of time; an historian.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
TEACH, v.t. To instruct; to inform; to communicate to another the knowledge of that of which he was before ignorant.
TUTOR, n. One who has the care of instructing another in various branches of learning.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; the choice of laudable ends, and of the best means to accomplish them.
scriptures: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.
corruption_summary: Carinthia's first Cistercian house, 1142, home of the chronicler John of Viktring and since 1786 a school.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that chronicling and teaching are one trade, the handing on of what was received. Viktring did both for six centuries, and the duty is first laid on parents at perfectly ordinary hours, “and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deu 6:7).

The live temptation is to let an institution absorb a duty it cannot discharge, so that the school is credited with what belongs to a household. The psalmist states the obligation as a refusal, “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4); the curriculum begins with a disposition, “and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Pro 9:10); and the examination is practical, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psa 111:10).

pos: n. (the Tyrolean Cistercian abbey of 1273, founded by Elizabeth of Bavaria after the execution of her son Conradin)
etymology: Romance stabulum, a standing-place or stable, through a local dialect form.
biblical_def: Stams in the upper Inn valley was founded in 1273 by Elizabeth of Bavaria and her second husband Meinhard II of Tyrol, and the occasion was a grief: Elizabeth's son by her first marriage was Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, beheaded at Naples in 1268 at the age of sixteen. She endowed the abbey for the repose of his soul, and it became the burial church of the Tyrolean princes, with a baroque reconstruction and a famous Gothic grille over the princes' tombs. The dictionary names the arrangement with the honour due to the grief and the plainness due to the error. A mother's sorrow is not the corruption; the theology sold to her was. An abbey endowed to shorten a dead boy's suffering trades on a treasury Scripture does not grant, and Christ's word to the thief settles both the timing and the agency, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Luk 23:43). The work that secures it is already finished and complete, “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). The advocate is in place and needs no deputy, “who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:34), and the name that saves is exclusive, “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines purgatory as a supposed place of temporary suffering; a requiem as a mass for the dead; suffrage in this sense as prayer offered for another; a treasury as a place where treasure is kept; and absolution as the act of absolving from sin.
webster_full: PURGATORY, n. Among catholics, a supposed place or state where souls are purified after death, before they ascend to heaven.
REQUIEM, n. A hymn or mass sung for the dead, for the rest of his soul.
SUFFRAGE, n. A vote; also, in church use, a short prayer or intercession offered for another.
TREASURY, n. A place or building in which stores of wealth are reposited; a place where public revenues are deposited.
ABSOLUTION, n. In the civil law, an acquittal of a person accused; in the church, the remission of sins pronounced by a priest.
scriptures: And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: Tyrolean Cistercian abbey of 1273 endowed by Elizabeth of Bavaria for the soul of her executed son Conradin.
corruption_paragraphs: Elizabeth of Bavaria had her sixteen-year-old son beheaded in a Neapolitan square and founded an abbey for his soul. The dictionary grants the grief its full weight and names the doctrine sold to her as the corruption it was. A foundation endowed to shorten a dead boy's purgation assumes a treasury of merit and a postponement of the verdict; Christ's word to a dying man beside Him allows neither, “Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Luk 23:43).

The corruption is still taught. Rome defines purgatory as a state of purification after death and commends suffrages for the dead, and indulgences are still attached to them. Scripture closes every door the system needs open: the offering is already perfect and in the past, “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever” (Heb 10:14); the intercessor is in post and requires no help, “It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again” (Rom 8:34); and the saving name is exclusive of every other, “Neither is there salvation in any other” (Act 4:12).

pos: n. (the Upper Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1355, a nunnery then a monastery, keeping a stained-glass workshop)
etymology: German Schlierbach, the muddy brook, from Schlier, marl or mud, and Bach.
biblical_def: Schlierbach in Upper Austria was founded in 1355 as a Cistercian nunnery by Eberhard of Wallsee, emptied by plague and the Reformation, and refounded in 1620 as a house of monks from Rein. Its church was rebuilt in stucco baroque by the Carlone family. Since 1864 the abbey has run a stained-glass workshop, one of the few monastic glass studios still working, which has made and repaired windows for churches across Europe; it also keeps a dairy and makes cheese. The dictionary records Schlierbach for the glass, because a window is a device for admitting light that it does not make. Fellowship among Christians is described in exactly that dependent way, as a walking in light already shining, “But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another” (1Jo 1:7). The light believers are said to give out is to be seen and traced to its source, “that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16). The text itself is the illumination of the untaught, “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130), and the lamp that can be trusted in the dark is a word rather than an impression, “a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines glass as a hard brittle transparent substance; to glaze as to furnish with glass; a window as an opening for the admission of light; a workshop as a shop where work is performed; and a dairy as a place where milk is set for cream.
webster_full: GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies.
GLAZE, v.t. To furnish with windows of glass; to incrust with a vitreous substance.
WINDOW, n. An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light, and of air when necessary.
WORKSHOP, n. A shop where any manufacture or handywork is carried on.
DAIRY, n. The place, room or house where milk is set for cream, and where butter and cheese are made.
scriptures: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Cistercian house, a nunnery of 1355 refounded for monks in 1620, running a working stained-glass studio since 1864.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a window admits light it did not make. Schlierbach's studio has glazed churches across Europe for a century and a half, and the apostolic figure for fellowship is exactly this kind of dependence, “as he is in the light” (1Jo 1:7).

The live temptation is to credit the glass with the sun, which is what a beautiful church does to a congregation with no doctrine. Christ directs the attention through the works to the Father, “Let your light so shine before men” (Mat 5:16); the illumination of a plain reader is the text, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130); and the lamp to steer by at night is a word and not a feeling, “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed” (2Pe 1:19).

pos: n. (the Upper Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1146, rebuilt after the fire of 1733 as the finest rococo church in Austria)
etymology: German Wilhering, from an Old High German personal name Wilher.
biblical_def: Wilhering on the Danube above Linz was founded in 1146 by the lords of Wilhering and settled from Rein, and the community has been there since, apart from one vacancy in the fifteenth century. On the third of March 1733 the whole abbey burned except the Gothic doorway and part of the cloister. The monks rebuilt, and what they put up is the most completely realised rococo interior in Austria: Bartolomeo Altomonte's ceilings, the Schmidt brothers' stucco, a nave that reads as one continuous ornament. The dictionary records Wilhering for the rebuilding, because Scripture has a great deal to say about building again on a burnt site. The promise to those who do it is explicit, “And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4), and the prophet of a second temple was given a word about its glory that deliberately exceeds the first, “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former” (Hag 2:9). The means are named so that no builder may claim them, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and the burning itself is reported in Scripture as a grief rather than an opportunity, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rococo in the sense of fantastic ornament; stucco as a fine plaster for walls; a fresco as a painting on fresh plaster; conflagration as a great fire; and to rebuild as to build again.
webster_full: STUCCO, n. A fine plaster, composed of lime, sand and marble dust, used for walls and ceilings.
FRESCO, n. A method of painting on walls with water colors, on fresh plaster, or on a wall laid with mortar not yet dry.
CONFLAGRATION, n. A great fire, or the burning of any great mass of combustibles.
REBUILD, v.t. To build again; to renew a structure; to build or restore after destruction.

scriptures: And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1146 burned to the ground in 1733 and rebuilt as Austria's finest rococo interior.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that rebuilding after a fire is a scriptural office with a promise attached. Wilhering lost everything but a doorway in 1733 and rebuilt within a generation, and the word spoken over such work is plain, “they shall repair the waste cities” (Isa 61:4).

The live temptation is to credit the result to the builders, which an interior of that brilliance makes very easy. Haggai's promise about a second house exceeding the first is spoken by the LORD and not by the masons, “saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9); Zechariah names the agency so that nobody may mistake it, “This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel” (Zec 4:6); and the fire is never treated as a favour, “they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7).

pos: n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1182, a daughter of Clairvaux, destroyed by the Turks and refounded as a teaching house)
etymology: Hungarian Zirc, from a Slavic or Hungarian personal name.
biblical_def: Zirc in the Bakony hills was founded in 1182 by Bela III and settled directly from Clairvaux, the chief Cistercian house of Hungary. The Ottoman wars destroyed it: the community was scattered in the sixteenth century and the buildings fell, and for over a hundred years there was nothing there. From 1700 the Cistercians of Heinrichau and then Lilienfeld rebuilt it, and in the nineteenth century Zirc became the head of a Hungarian congregation that ran secondary schools across the country until the suppressions of 1950. Its library hall is among the finest in Hungary. The dictionary records Zirc for the long interval, because Scripture speaks about the rebuilding of a razed sanctuary as something God does rather than something a nation manages, “When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory” (Psa 102:16). The human part of such work begins with a frank look at the rubble, “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste” (Neh 2:17), and when a foundation is laid again the proper noise is thanksgiving, “because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid” (Ezr 3:11). The century with nothing standing is covered by a different instruction altogether, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restoration as the act of replacing in a former state; a congregation in this sense as an association of religious houses; suppression as the act of putting down; a gymnasium as a higher school; and to await as to wait for, to expect.
webster_full: RESTORATION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; revival; re-establishment.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for worship.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or putting down; concealment.
GYMNASIUM, n. In Germany, a school of the higher order, in which the languages and sciences are taught.
AWAIT, v.t. To wait for; to look for, or expect; to attend, as a consequence.
scriptures: When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.

And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Hungary's chief Cistercian house, 1182, a daughter of Clairvaux, razed by the Ottomans and rebuilt from 1700 as a teaching congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the rebuilding of a sanctuary is God's act before it is a nation's project. Zirc lay in ruins for over a century, and the psalmist assigns the agency without qualification, “When the LORD shall build up Zion” (Psa 102:16).

The live temptation is impatience during the interval, and then self-congratulation once the scaffolding goes up. Nehemiah models the first corrective, a plain look at the damage, “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17); Ezra the second, which is thanksgiving at a relaid foundation, “because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel” (Ezr 3:11); and the long wait between has its own commendation, “and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

“quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26) — the instruction for the long interval.

pos: n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1184, burial place of Queen Gertrude of Merania, now an excavated ruin)
etymology: Hungarian Pilis, from a Slavic root for a bare or bald hill.
biblical_def: Pilis in the hills north-west of Budapest was founded in 1184 by Bela III and settled from Acey in Burgundy, and became one of the richest houses in the kingdom and a favourite of the court. Queen Gertrude of Merania, wife of Andrew II, was murdered by Hungarian nobles in 1213 and buried at Pilis under a tomb of French workmanship whose fragments have been recovered; the killing is the historical seed of the Bank ban story that became Hungary's national drama. The Ottomans destroyed the abbey and nothing now stands above foundation level. The dictionary records Pilis for the murder, because a crime in a royal court is where Scripture's demand for justice stops being an abstraction. God rejects a worship offered over an unjust society in terms that are deliberately offensive, “I hate, I despise your feast days” (Amo 5:21), and names what He wants instead in the figure of a river, “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream” (Amo 5:24). The whole requirement is reducible to three terms, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8), and the civil order charged with enforcing the first of them is God's own ordinance, “For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justice as the virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; regicide as the murder of a king; vengeance as the infliction of pain in return for an injury; equity as impartiality; and a magistrate as a public civil officer.
webster_full: JUSTICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; practical conformity to the laws.
REGICIDE, n. The murder or murderer of a king; the killing of a king.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.
EQUITY, n. Justice; right; impartiality; the giving to each man his due.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
scriptures: I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies.
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1184 where Queen Gertrude of Merania was buried after her murder in 1213, now an excavated ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship offered over an unpunished crime is refused. Pilis buried a murdered queen and went on singing, and the prophet's language for that arrangement is calculated to offend, “and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies” (Amo 5:21).

The live temptation at a royal abbey is a devotion that functions as a substitute for justice rather than as its root. Amos puts the alternative in a figure of moving water rather than of ceremony, “righteousness as a mighty stream” (Amo 5:24); Micah compresses the whole demand into three terms, “what doth the LORD require of thee” (Mic 6:8); and the magistracy charged with the first of them holds its commission from God, “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).

pos: n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1190, formerly Benedictine, keeping a medieval glassworks and school)
etymology: Hungarian Paszto, probably from pasztor, a shepherd, or a personal name.
biblical_def: Paszto in northern Hungary was a Benedictine house that passed to the Cistercians in 1190, settled from Pilis, and it is unusual among Hungarian abbeys for what the excavations found: a medieval glassworks with furnaces and crucibles, and the foundations of a school building, both inside the monastic precinct. The abbey ran a mill on the Zagyva and kept vineyards on the hillside. It was ruined in the Ottoman wars and partly rebuilt in the eighteenth century. The dictionary records Paszto for its workshops, because a monastery with a furnace in the yard is a standing argument against the division of life into sacred and secular hours. Work is the ordinary appointment of fallen man and is nowhere treated as beneath him, “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), and the apostolic rule for a community of believers is bluntly practical, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). The proverb promises a return and contrasts it with talk, “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23). What Scripture does question is spending on what does not feed, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crucible as a melting pot for metals; a furnace as a place where a vehement fire is maintained; a mill as a machine for grinding; a vineyard as a plantation of vines; and penury as want, extreme poverty.
webster_full: CRUCIBLE, n. A melting pot, made of earth, and used by chemists and others for melting metals.
FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire and heat may be made and maintained, for melting ores or other substances.
MILL, n. A complicated engine or machine for grinding and reducing to fine particles, grain, fruit or other substance.
VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; an inclosure devoted to the culture of grapes.
PENURY, n. Want of property; indigence; extreme poverty.
scriptures: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
corruption_summary: Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1190 with a medieval glassworks, a school, a mill and vineyards inside the precinct.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a furnace in a monastic yard refutes the division of hours into sacred and secular. Paszto blew glass and ground corn beside its choir, and work is presented in Scripture as the common appointment of men rather than a lower calling, “till thou return unto the ground” (Gen 3:19).

The live temptation runs both ways, toward a contemplation that despises the forge and toward an industry that forgets why it was lit. The apostolic rule settles the first, “this we commanded you” (2Th 3:10); the proverb promises the forge a return and gives idle talk none, “but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23); and the prophet questions not the labour but its object, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2).
